contributions.item_title_en: 8. Short Debate: Green across the aisle: Making environmental stewardship a common cause
contributions.text_english: Thank you very much, Llywydd. Could I start by thanking the Member for tabling this debate and giving us the opportunity to discuss this topic once again, and also to the other Members for their contributions this afternoon? We don't always agree in this Chamber, but I do agree with the central proposal behind today's debate, which is, of course, that environmental stewardship is not the responsibility of just one party. It is not the responsibility of one sector or even one generation. It's a shared responsibility, and the potential benefits of that reach every community in Wales, whether that is clean rivers, healthy soils, productive farms, nature recovery, clean energy, stronger local economies. These aren't competing priorities. They are all connected, in my view, and that understanding, of course, is at the heart of this Government's programme for government. It shapes our approach to farming, water, clean energy, rural resilience. It also shapes the way that we create the conditions for sustainable growth, and, of course, we focus on practical delivery—not stewardship as a theory, but stewardship in practice, on the ground.

contributions.item_title_en: 8. Short Debate: Green across the aisle: Making environmental stewardship a common cause
contributions.text_english:
We're developing, as Members know, Wales's first climate and nature action plan. It'll bring together actions across government and across society to restore nature, to strengthen climate resilience, to support sustainable development, setting out a pathway towards our ambition in relation to net zero, but also substantive nature recovery as well. And a just transition will be baked into our approach, so that we avoid some of the mistakes that have happened in the past where some communities have been damaged and left behind by much of this.

And I would refer to an example that I've used previously when it comes to this. Retrofitting homes is one policy that's being put forward as a means of reducing carbon emissions. But, of course, it isn't a binary policy, because retrofitting homes provides people with support for the cost-of-living crisis because it will lower bills. More energy-efficient homes will mean lower energy bills. Retrofitting homes means jobs. People will need to be employed to retrofit those homes, bringing further economic benefits. It'll give people warmer homes to live in. And that, in itself, I think is something that we should aspire to. But there are health benefits from that as well, because we will see, as a consequence of people not living in cold and damp homes, fewer children being raised in those homes and consequently suffering from respiratory challenges. We will see fewer winter excess deaths amongst our older population. So, net zero isn't binary. It's an opportunity to bring a number of additional benefits with it.

And environmental stewardship as well can't sit within one portfolio. Decisions on housing, on transport, on food production, on skills, on economic development, public investment, they all matter. Every part of Government has a role here. And that ambition, of course, has to be backed up then by strong governance and accountability. And the Environment (Principles, Governance and Biodiversity Targets) (Wales) Act 2026 creates, doesn't it, the independent Office of Environmental Governance Wales to monitor environmental law, and hold public authorities to account. Statutory biodiversity targets will provide the long-term focus and transparency needed to halt and reverse biodiversity loss. And we'll develop those, by the way, using science and evidence. Taken together, the legislation, the independent oversight and targets give us a strong foundation for long-term nature recovery.

Now, farmers are at the heart of much of this approach, but not just only farmers. There's a wider societal piece that's playing out here as well. But farmers do manage, of course, most of the land in Wales and they play a vital role as stewards of our countryside. Many of the habitats and landscapes we value depend on that active management. They produce our food, they sustain rural businesses and communities, and help shape the landscape that defines Wales very often.

Too often, these debates present a choice, don't they, between food production and nature recovery. Well, the sustainable farming scheme is built on a simple principle: resilient ecosystems and sustainable food production can and should go hand in hand. And this year, as we know, more than 8,000 farm businesses, around half of all eligible farms in Wales, have joined the universal layer of the SFS. Now, that is a strong foundation on which to refine the scheme and develop future optional and collaborative actions. And the reason I didn't directly answer the points raised is because we haven't made those decisions yet. Those discussions are still ongoing, because I want to hear the voices of those around the table in stakeholder groups, and I want to understand what the options are. But when we have made the decision, you will be amongst the first to know.

So, as I've said, this whole process is evolution, isn't it? It's evolution, not revolution. Farmers need certainty because they plan over many years—we know that—and that's why I've committed to over £1 billion over three years, to a multi-year funding cycle for the SFS, giving the sector that long-term certainty it needs to be able to help it to plan and invest with confidence. But support must also be practical. Good stewardship should not come with unnecessary bureaucracy, and, as you know, I have commissioned an independent review of the bureaucratic burden on family farms to identify where there is unnecessary complexity and to recommend practical improvements, because by reducing duplication and simplifying processes, we can then help farmers focus on what really matters most, which is the point I think that you're making: running successful businesses, producing food and caring for the landscapes that they manage.

But individual action, of course, is only part of the answer. Flooding, water quality, wildfires and nature recovery don't stop at field boundaries, and that's why collaboration matters here as well. Through the collaborative layer of the sustainable farming scheme, we are looking to create those opportunities for farmers, land managers and communities to work together across landscapes and across catchments. The integrated natural resources scheme is demonstrating the value of collaboration as well across those larger landscapes and catchments, to improve water quality, to restore habitats, to reduce flood risk, of course, which is important here as well, and to strengthen that climate resilience that we need to build. We're now looking at how we can build on that approach and strengthen the support for that collaborative action in the future.

Ffermio Bro supports co-ordinated action within our designated landscapes, helping farmers and land managers deliver local priorities for nature recovery, for ecosystem resilience and climate action. Its funding has increased from £1.9 million in 2025-26 to £7.5 million from 2026-28. Together, these schemes hopefully will shape future collaborative delivery through the sustainable farming scheme and other means, enabling action at a scale that no individual holding can achieve alone.

We're also looking to restore Wales's natural assets as well. Peatlands are among our most important carbon stores, and wildlife habitats too. The national peatland action programme has restored over 4,000 hectares and has improved the habitat across a further 9,000 hectares here in Wales. That work supports biodiversity, yes, it does store carbon, whether we like it or not, but it also improves water management and it strengthens resilience to drought, flooding and wildfires—again, the multilayered benefits of some of these actions that we're taking. It's practical delivery for climate and nature together.

But restoration can't be limited to individual habitats or protected sites. Nature recovery is needed across productive farmland, yes, but in our towns and communities as well. And, of course, Government can't deliver all of this alone. Through Nature Networks, we've announced more than £10 million for the next funding round. The fund has already supported more than 125 projects, improving protected sites and ecological connections across Wales.

For example, this year Natural Resources Wales updated flood risk mapping at eight river locations across Wales. They also delivered improvements to their live flood warning service. NRW flood warnings and severe weather warnings are now available on a greater number of third-party digital platforms. This will therefore, of course, increase the visibility of NRW flood warnings, supporting public awareness.

As a Government, we have made almost £5 million of revenue funding available to local authorities for flood risk activities. Across Wales, they are preparing for the winter months. This includes assessing key assets, jetting drains and managing vegetation to reduce blockage risks. They are also reviewing emergency response arrangements to ensure that they remain effective.

Our national security and resilience team continues to monitor and assess all risks over the winter, including winter weather. It works with resilience partners to ensure that there's a shared understanding to support informed resilience planning across Wales.

This year, as always, our preparations are grounded in the lessons learned from previous storms. Last November, storm Claudia brought significant rainfall across Wales. The storm impacted almost 400 properties in Monmouthshire alone. Some locations saw flood depths of more than 1.5m. Communities, infrastructure and essential services were disrupted.

I understand how devastating flooding can be for households and businesses. In August of this year, I visited Milford Haven, where I heard first-hand from residents affected by flooding and discussed plans for a new flood scheme to better protect their properties. It was a powerful reminder of why this work matters.

So, let me highlight some of the ways in which we will, as a Government, support our communities and partners. We are giving flood-affected communities a stronger voice through a new independent Welsh flood forum. The new forum will support communities recovering from flooding and will strengthen preparedness and resilience for future events. It will be based on the successful model implemented in Scotland, and I can confirm that the forum’s steering group met for the first time last week. It brought together people with lived experience of flooding and partner organisations. Collectively, they will help shape a new national support network for flood-affected communities. 

We will also shortly appoint additional members to the flood and coastal erosion committee, ensuring it can continue to provide independent advice to Welsh Ministers and, in so doing, help us to shape future policy.

This Government understands the importance of continued investment in our flood risk management infrastructure, making over £85 million available in this year alone. This funding will support communities by delivering interventions ranging from flood defences to community engagement activities. It will also provide long-term flood protection and support increased resilience to climate change. Examples include schemes at Edward Street in Ystrad Mynach; Maesyffynnon Lane in Rhondda Cynon Taf; Llandysul and Pont Tyweli in Carmarthenshire; School Bank Road in Llanrwst; and Bontnewydd in Gwynedd.

Wherever possible, we encourage risk management authorities to consider investment in natural flood management interventions. These interventions complement the natural environment and help slow the movement of water through catchments, whilst improving water quality and strengthening biodiversity. Interventions can then be targeted where they are most effective, not only for communities but also for the environment.

But natural flood management can only succeed through strong partnership working with farmers and landowners. The sustainable farming scheme will be an important part of this. It will help land managers to adopt nature-based solutions, which reduce flood risk and support wider environmental and climate resilience outcomes. However, despite this continued investment, it is essential that communities remain vigilant to the risk of flooding and are prepared for all eventualities. One in seven properties in Wales is at risk of flooding, but only 27 per cent of those householders are registered to receive NRW's flood warnings.

This week, NRW is running its annual Be Flood Ready campaign. Many of you will perhaps have seen that on social media in recent days. The campaign highlights three simple steps that everyone can take to be better prepared for flooding. Firstly, you should check your property's flood risk, and you can do that online. NRW's website allows people to check flood-risk information using their postcode and an interactive map. Secondly, then sign up for free flood warnings, from both rivers and the sea. Warnings can be received via text messages, e-mail or voicemail messages, and people can register through NRW's website or by contacting Floodline, and I will share the number: it's 0345 988 1188. And finally, be prepared when flooding is forecast. NRW provides practical online advice to help people prepare for, to respond to, and then, of course, to recover from flooding. And I encourage everyone to make use of these free resources. Please do check if you or your family are at risk of flooding, and, if you are, please then access all the support available to you.

I also encourage everyone to review their insurance arrangements. Flood cover is not always included in standard household insurance policies. It is therefore important to check the details of your cover. Some new policies may not take effect immediately, so acting early can be crucial in that regard. And for those who find it difficult to obtain cover, I would like to highlight two specific schemes. The first is Flood Re. This UK-wide scheme helps households access affordable flood insurance, and it may be particularly relevant, of course, to people who have previously experienced flooding or who have struggled to obtain insurance cover. The Flood Re website provides details of participating insurers, but I encourage people to consider their options carefully. And the second is the build back better scheme. This allows householders recovering from flooding to install flood resilience measures in their property during the repair process, and up to £10,000 may be available from insurers to support these improvements.

But in looking ahead, Dirprwy Lywydd, preparation remains our strongest defence against flooding and severe weather. The Welsh Government will continue to work closely with partners to strengthen resilience, to learn, of course, from past events, and to support our communities, and I want to thank everyone involved in that work. By working together, we can help ensure that Wales is ready for the challenges this winter may bring. Thank you.

Well, I was minded to thank the spokesperson for her response, but I do rather feel that it doesn't appreciate what is already happening. You know, £85 million is a significant chunk of Welsh Government funding towards flood schemes. You referenced Monmouthshire. Diolch yn fawr. There's a lot there. Certainly, in terms of informing people about the risks and actions they can take, I hope that this statement today will contribute to that. contributions.item_title_en: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability: Winter preparedness: Be flood ready
contributions.text_english:
Thank you very much, again, a long list of questions there. I think it was right that you acknowledged the impact on businesses as well, because we do focus, of course, on domestic properties and homes, but businesses, absolutely. And I would reiterate again that there are particular sources of support and the need for different kinds of insurances, et cetera, for businesses as well, and there is information out there to support those, similarly.

You asked about the overall picture and what it would cost to fix it all. I don't have that figure. What I do know is that 273,000 properties are at risk in Wales, and not one Government can meet the cost of addressing all of that. But that is, of course, why we are pursuing—building on work from previous Governments as well—nature finance and those opportunities that, hopefully, will allow us to invest in those catchment-scale, nature-based solutions that will go part of the way in defending and mitigating some of those risks.

The resilience of services is absolutely critical here. In fact, the wider Cabinet yesterday spent some time considering wider resilience questions here in Wales. The First Minister himself, of course, has an overarching responsibility for national resilience, but you're right, it's about working with other Ministers and we do that and we will continue to do that. And, of course, that will come into greater focus again on the back of the summit, where I hope there will be some clear outcomes, some clear actions for us all to pursue collectively.

Only 27 per cent are registered for the NRW alerts. When I chaired the climate change committee in the last Senedd, we published a report on flooding and the response to flooding; this was one of the concerns that we highlighted. I'm glad to see a concerted effort now from NRW to increase and to try and promote that, but of course, that isn't just on NRW, it's for every single one of us here as well to make sure that we use our social media channels, that we use our contacts and connections in communities, particularly in those communities that people have referred to that we know are facing potential risks this winter. So, I would not just throw it back to you, but I would say that we all have a part to play in that endeavour.

But also, of course, we are, I will remind Members, in the process of setting up the Welsh flood forum, which is going to be all about making sure that communities are prepared, and then when something happens, that there is a response and a resilience from within, not just from the emergency authorities, but also the support there to recover as well. We're taking inspiration from what they've done in Scotland and we're engaging with the National Flood Forum to start that work in earnest. As I said, I was part of a meeting last week where we brought those stakeholders together with those people from communities with lived experience of flooding to start the work of bringing all of this together.

Thank you for your question, and you're right, there's a longer term picture here, and there's a shorter term, more initial response that's required, and we try and accommodate that in the way that we utilise the funding that's available. So, as I said, this year we are making £85 million available to risk management authorities across Wales. That includes nearly £30 million in revenue funding for things like asset maintenance, warning systems, which are absolutely relevant this year, operational planning and flood response, which all could be part of the services provided within the coming months. Once those schemes are completed, then the estimate is that that funding will benefit over 7,000 properties.

contributions.item_title_en: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
contributions.text_english:
Thank you for that question. I know that this is a challenge that could occur in a number of different contexts. I hope you'll be reassured that the Welsh Government is working with Natural Resources Wales and local planning authorities through the planning and environmental permitting systems to make sure that groundwater risks are identified and that they are properly assessed and managed before major developments proceed.

We set the national planning policy framework that local planning authorities apply when determining applications, and Natural Resources Wales provide specialist technical advice on groundwater risks as a statutory consultee. Planning authorities can draw on their hydrogeological expertise when they consider whether further investigation or any mitigation or monitoring is needed before a decision is taken. 

Where evidence identifies a specific local risk, local planning authorities and NRW can use their respective planning and permitting functions to make sure that proportionate monitoring and controls are in place during construction and operation. But, ultimately, we will work closely with those bodies to support the consistent and effective application of groundwater protections as a number of different development pressures—and environmental risks, no doubt—evolve.

contributions.text_english:

The Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning and I both recognise the importance of this issue. 

To strengthen leadership and strategic co-ordination to try and address those nutrient-related challenges, the Welsh Government is establishing a new nutrient efficiency and resilience group. That group will bring together key partners and stakeholders, including regulators, water companies, the agricultural sector, environmental organisations and local authority representatives, to provide strategic oversight of nutrient management across Wales.

Its work will focus on both the immediate operational challenges, which are pressing, but also the longer term actions needed to restore and improve the health of our rivers and catchments, helping to deliver a more co-ordinated and whole-system approach to river recovery and environmental improvement, but also, hopefully, unlocking potential developments such as the one that you've referred to.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Contaminated land
contributions.text_english:
However, I also agree with the motion that at the heart of this issue is a simple, simple principle: those responsible for pollution should cover the costs of putting that harm right. Now, the polluter-pays principle is an important safeguard for communities and for taxpayers, and I believe it's an essential part of delivering environmental justice.

I recognise that determining contaminated land liability can be challenging for regulators. Some of these sites we're dealing with, as we've heard today, relate to activities from decades ago, even hundreds of years ago, and that can mean that there's often little evidence left behind to link the contamination to the polluter. Indeed, the polluter may no longer even still exist. Yet, despite these challenges, I'm keen to strengthen this core principle, and we will work closely with regulators and the UK Government and, indeed, others on an international level, over the coming months, to identify the options that we have to get to grips with this properly.

On the point of working with others, I welcome the numerous calls for the UK Government to play their role in addressing these issues as well. I'm under no illusion that, in the absence of any polluter being able to pay, then dealing with the legacy of contaminated land will require sustained investment. However, communities that have lived with these issues for many years rightly expect us to work together to deliver those lasting solutions. So, we've already seen what we can achieve through the joint commitment of the Welsh and UK Governments on coal tip safety that a number of Members have referred to, and I believe that that gives us a strong case for a similar approach here. This partnership hasn't only helped to address coal tip safety, but also has removed the economic burden on coalfield communities as well, and I am keen that this model is something that, hopefully, we can adopt in this context as well.

contributions.text_english:
That's why, of course, we are continuing to press the UK Treasury on the importance of providing funding to support our joint efforts to address this legacy, through both the restoration of coal tips, yes, but also the remediation of contaminated land, as highlighted in the debate today. And I know that the First Minister has written to the Prime Minister, encouraging him to engage to develop this joint endeavour. I'm also aware that the finance Minister raised this with the previous Chief Secretary to the Treasury, as well, of course, more recently on more than one occasion with the current incumbent as well. I can also confirm that we will be making the case to HM Treasury to secure funding for this work at next year’s UK spending review.

Turning now to the request for a national framework, I recognise concerns have been raised about how sites are assessed and the need for more testing. Part 2A of the Environmental Protection Act 1990 is the statutory regime for contaminated land in Wales. Local authorities are the lead regulators and have a statutory responsibility to identify and, as well, to prioritise sites in their areas. This will be based on local knowledge and different assessments that they undertake.

Whilst I want to avoid duplication or, indeed, undermining the importance of that local expertise, I am supportive of exploring a possible all-Wales approach to site prioritisation. For example, I understand that individual local authorities may actually use different parameters and different tools to risk-assess a site. Well, really, could there not be merit in adopting a standardised approach for all, so that we all know where we stand, and that it's done on a consistent basis? So, that is certainly something that I will be exploring further with my officials.

It's also important to note, of course, that, for a site to be designated contaminated land, it needs to be causing, or having the potential to cause, significant harm to human health or the environment. Now, the legislation adopts a risk-based approach. So, in simple terms, land contamination only becomes a Part 2A problem when there is something harmful, and then a way for it to move, and something that can be harmed by it. Remove any one of these, and the risk linkage is broken.

However, I recognise that, whilst this approach is intended to ensure those sites causing direct risks are prioritised, it can create uncertainty when a site is not legally defined as contaminated land. I am keen to see how these sites are considered to explore how we consider that, and whether a wider, again, national framework could capture such sites if a legitimate burden is being placed on a community or a local authority.

I also understand, of course, that people living near polluted sites want answers. Why wouldn't they? Of course they do. And they want reassurance as well when it comes to their health particularly, and I'm aware that Public Health Wales is working with its partners, including health boards, local authorities and Natural Resources Wales, to review the concerns raised in the BBC Buried programme.

I also understand Public Health Wales have urged caution in relation to calls for widespread blood testing for PCBs, noting the limitations and the barriers to adopting this type of approach. They've noted that managing current and future risks to the population should involve a focus on identifying and containing potential routes of exposure to PCBs from sites of concern.

Finally, on the call to support local authorities with their statutory responsibilities, I've already asked my officials to provide options as to how best to achieve this. I recognise that individual local authorities will have different levels of resource and different levels of experience available to them. I want to make sure that any support we may provide is reflective of these differing needs so that everyone is able to benefit, regardless of the capacity of their local authority.  

Once again, I welcome this opportunity today to engage with Members on this issue, and to listen the concerns that have been raised. I've certainly been making notes and I'll be looking to see how some these issues can be directly addressed. As previously noted, this is, of course, a complex area, with many years of evidence gathering and research undertaken to help regulators. Consequently, some changes may take longer than others to make. However, despite these potential challenges, we as a Government are absolutely committed to developing a Wales-wide strategy to progressively restore post-industrial land and to protect communities from those potential risks that come with that legacy. I hear the calls for action and I will ensure that former industrial land is made safe. I'll protect public health and deliver long-overdue environmental justice for the communities that have been most affected by this. I look forward to all Members, hopefully, supporting this motion today and to help continue this journey to protect both people's health and the environment for future generations. Diolch.

So, in simple terms, land contamination only becomes a Part 2A problem when there is something harmful, and then a way for it to move, and something that can be harmed by it. Remove any one of these, and the risk linkage is broken.

However, I recognise that, whilst this approach is intended to ensure those sites causing direct risks are prioritised, it can create uncertainty when a site is not legally defined as contaminated land. I am keen to see how these sites are considered to explore how we consider that, and whether a wider, again, national framework could capture such sites if a legitimate burden is being placed on a community or a local authority.

I also understand, of course, that people living near polluted sites want answers. Why wouldn't they? Of course they do. And they want reassurance as well when it comes to their health particularly, and I'm aware that Public Health Wales is working with its partners, including health boards, local authorities and Natural Resources Wales, to review the concerns raised in the BBC Buried programme.

I also understand Public Health Wales have urged caution in relation to calls for widespread blood testing for PCBs, noting the limitations and the barriers to adopting this type of approach. They've noted that managing current and future risks to the population should involve a focus on identifying and containing potential routes of exposure to PCBs from sites of concern.

I recognise that individual local authorities will have different levels of resource and different levels of experience available to them. contributions.item_title_en: 6. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability: Update on the Deposit-return Scheme
contributions.text_english:
The scheme will include metal and plastic drinks containers from day 1. Glass containers will also be in scope from day 1, but reflecting our manifesto commitment, we will work closely with Exchange for Change, and the wider drinks industry, on a pragmatic approach to glass. This includes the four-year transition period, during which no deposit will apply and in which no DRS-specific labelling will be required, as well as the phased introduction of reuse.  

Working with Exchange for Change, our focus is now on the scheme’s implementation by October next year, and on supporting businesses, delivery partners and consumers to be ready for launch. In doing so, we will work to ensure Wales secures the benefits of the scheme, including reduced litter, the capture of high-quality materials for recycling back into the economy, and a clear pathway towards the roll-out of reuse. The coverage of all materials ensures that the scheme can tackle the litter seen on our streets and in our communities, of all drinks container types, from the outset. It also means that we can not only retain more valuable materials within the economy, but it also puts in place a pathway to the roll-out of reusable drinks containers, and the benefits the best schemes in the world are already delivering internationally.

Litter is not only a blight on our communities, it also imposes costs on local authorities, on taxpayers and on land managers as well. As DRS has been proven to do in other countries, by preventing litter and capturing drinks containers of all material types, it'll not only keep the materials from polluting the environment, or posing a hazard to people and wildlife, but it'll also reduce the burden of litter management and clean-up activities.

With Wales having experienced significant wildfire incidents this summer, as climate change increases, it is important as well to avoid preventable sources of ignition. With the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service having identified discarded glass bottles as one potential cause of wildfires—as sunlight passing through glass can, of course, focus heat onto dry vegetation and ignite fires—it is a reminder of the risks that littered glass in particular can present.

A successful deposit-return scheme will therefore help deliver cleaner communities and public spaces in our town centres, parks, beaches and countryside. As a Government, supporting businesses, particularly our small and medium-sized enterprises, to successfully transition and benefit from the scheme is a priority. We will therefore work with Exchange for Change to ensure that small and medium-sized businesses are fully engaged as we progress to implementation.

The success of the scheme depends on the participation of businesses of all sizes, and the regulations therefore include low-volume producer exemptions, exemptions as well for smaller retailers where that's appropriate, and flexible return arrangements. Together, these measures provide certainty and reduce compliance costs, and the four-year transition period, of course, for the deposit on glass also gives businesses more time to adapt.

Following on from the passing of the legislation by the Senedd earlier this year, the appointment of the deposit management organisation is a significant step forward to the delivery of DRS here in Wales.

contributions.text_english:
Maintaining current recycling performance is not the only aim of the scheme. contributions.text_english:
Well, what I would say initially is if we pause, if we wait, then I have no doubt that you would be on your feet then complaining about the risk of fraud. Because the rest of the UK is moving in this direction, okay? And everybody who was up in arms saying, 'Oh, if Wales isn’t moving in this direction then there will be fraud, there will be all sorts of problems and all sorts of concerns'—[Interruption.] The other parts of the UK would be the first to complain. So, we are all on a journey here, but what we have to recognise is that Wales is starting from a very different place.

We are asking producers, local authorities, consumers as well, to do something different. But if we are asking them to do something different, then we have to see a benefit from that, and including glass in the scheme is one benefit that we want to realise, because we need to keep that glass in the system. The one element that you have neglected, I think, in your analysis, is that this takes us closer to reuse. It's not about recycling. We need to move further up the waste hierarchy. Reuse would allow the same bottle to stay in use a number of times, reducing costs in terms of businesses that have to source those materials regularly. So, there are other benefits.

Littering, I mentioned in my statement. We have good records for recycling in the domestic space. We have regulations around improved recycling in business and in the workplace. On-the-go littering is a big problem, but this can be a big part of the answer, as we've seen from some of the international examples, where we can really bear down on on-the-go littering. A Keep Wales Tidy survey showed that drinks-related litter is on 43.6 per cent of our streets—nearly half of our streets are littered just by drinks-related litter. This can take us a step along that journey, reducing costs then, of course, for local authorities, for the work in terms of collecting some of that. And I mentioned the dangers from broken glass as well—well rehearsed. We know that there's more that we can and we need to do.

It's a deposit. It's a deposit; it's not an additional cost. Yes, those return points need to be accessible, of course they do, but there is no deposit payable in the first four years. This is a process of education, a process of working now with Exchange for Change to make those points as accessible and as easy to reach as possible. They won't only be in retail. I can imagine there'll be public spaces where those return points will be available as well. Where people tend to go or gather, we can provide them. And that as well is something that I think we need to keep in mind.

And council revenues, there are new waste streams coming online. Plastic film is one that's being trialled and developed now. There will be an additional stream of revenue coming for that. So, it's about striking that right balance.

The key thing for me coming from this statement today is that we now have a DMO here in Wales that brings us that partnership. That UK-wide partnership is embedded, really, because it's the same DMO that's delivering these services in all parts of the UK. And of course it's business led, it’s industry led; Exchange for Change is industry led. So, they can work with businesses, and we and others can make sure that we speak up for the communities as well in that process, as we work to delivering the operational model.

Some people want to scaremonger. There are legitimate issues that will need to be addressed over the next 12 months, but that's the point: we work up to October and the start date. I can't wait for us to get a point where, in five years' time, potentially, when the deposits kick in in terms of people paying, we will see a real material difference on the ground.

contributions.item_title_en: 6. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability: Update on the Deposit-return Scheme
contributions.text_english:
Thank you very much for welcoming this. Clearly, we're building on work that was done previously by our predecessor Government. It's something we inherited, but it's something we're embracing, and we're working hard to make sure that it works for everyone.

The biggest milestone is October next year, of course. That is when the scheme goes live across the UK. I know people have been concerned that we have been a little bit behind the curve in terms of appointing the DMO, so work is now happening on an official level to identify exactly how that is going to be achieved. I'm happy for a briefing to be held for Members—it's something I think we should do more of—just to sit down with Members, to respond to some of those concerns that some people are still raising, but also maybe to talk through the process in finer detail.

With the exemptions, you will be aware that some of the exemptions were outlined in regulations—from export shops to drinks supplied before the relevant commencement of the scheme. Small product lines are defined in the regulations, but also 'drink now' sales and hospitality. You will have situations where something is bought on premises, drunk on premises, so there are clear exemptions there. Again, I'm happy to write to you with that list in totality.

On the final point you made, the benefits of reuse are clear to us all. I touched earlier on the fact that it reduces costs in terms of having to source bottle after bottle and raw materials to produce those containers. But also there's a benefit in environmental terms in not having to keep creating those materials. But the quality of recycled material as well, when it is recycled, is much better, which, of course, is more valuable in terms of revenue streams. But keeping valuable resources like that in circulation for as long as possible is what we're trying to achieve here.

There are also additional economic benefits embedded in the whole process, because if we are reusing bottles, then we need reuse hubs, we need washeries, and those create jobs. I've seen a figure that a properly implemented DRS scheme would generate potentially up to 3,000 jobs across the UK. So, there are multiple benefits that we could realise here, but it is a transition. It's not going to happen overnight and neither should it, because things have to be introduced in a pragmatic and practical way. But that is the journey that we're on and one I'm determined to pursue.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you. There's quite a lot there. In terms of why include glass, given the costs involved and the implications for business, for local authorities and the changes in consumer behaviour that will be required, any scheme that we run in relation to DRS has to deliver meaningful additional benefits for Wales, rather than simply delivering what we already achieve. We need those tangible additional benefits, and without including glass, we don't see that, because we're recycling as we are—much of that is already happening—but we are going further because we do need to move in the direction of reuse, because that's what brings us greater prizes further down the line. 

You asked about the 10-week delay. There was a robust appointment process first of all—we needed to be confident that, in appointing Exchange for Change, it was the right decision. I am confident that that is the right decision. One benefit that that brings is that given that they are delivering similar schemes across other parts of the UK, they could hit the ground running. They're embedded in this sector; they understand what's needed. That, I think, will allow us to make sure that we can meet the October 2027 target in terms of going live.

On extended producer responsibility, including glass in DRS doesn't create an entirely new cost burden, because drinks producers using glass already meet producer responsibility obligations under the EPR scheme for packaging, meaning that many costs will transfer from EPR to the deposit-return scheme, rather than being an additional cost. Nation-specific reporting requirements are already in place under EPR, so it's not a new innovation when it comes to DRS as well.

You ask about UKIMA. I am confident that we are compliant with UKIMA. If you want to write to me with what you are suggesting, then I'll look at that, but I'm confident that we're not stepping outside the scope of that in what we intend to do. And there is a transition period. I won't repeat the point I made about the risk of fraud. The biggest risk of fraud is if there's no scheme here in Wales, and there will be.

As regards pubs and bars in the hospitality sector, I think I mentioned earlier that there are exemptions for 'drink on' sales in specified settings. Where deposit items are supplied for immediate consumption at mixed retail premises or on-sale premises such as hospitality, then there are flexibilities and exemptions there. So, again, it's something that we're mindful of, and as we develop the scheme, these are exactly the points that we need to be making sure that people understand.

contributions.item_title_en: 7. Reform UK Debate: Bovine TB
contributions.text_english:
There's no doubt that bovine TB is a highly complex, challenging and persistent disease. There is no single route of transmission and no simple solution. Cattle-to-cattle transmission remains a significant issue, but it is recognised that wildlife can also act as a source of infection, and that is why our response must be comprehensive and based on the evidence. As Members know, I recently announced my intention to refresh the TB eradication programme. The foundations of the current programme are strong, but we all now need to build on that progress and all step up our efforts if we're to achieve our ambition of a TB-free Wales by 2041.

I've met with the farming unions, with the British Veterinary Association, the TB programme board and the chair of the technical advisory group. Along with the wider technical advisory group membership, their combined expertise and advice will help shape the next phase of our approach. I agree that robust biosecurity standards and practices must remain a cornerstone of on-farm disease control. Effective biosecurity is a shared responsibility, with farmers and veterinarians working in partnership to prevent, detect and respond to disease threats, protecting animal health, livelihoods, public health and the resilience of our farms. But we must also be honest with ourselves. While biosecurity and cattle controls are essential, they're not the whole answer. If we are serious about achieving a TB-free Wales, we have to consider all sources of infection and all scientifically validated control measures available to us. This is why I agree that any future approach must recognise wildlife as one of several sources of infection that can contribute to the spread of bovine TB.

While I recognise that wildlife can play a role in the transmission of bovine TB, it is important that we don't pretend that wildlife is responsible in every case, nor should we prejudge the conclusions of our expert advisors. The technical advisory group is there to provide independent scientific expertise and advice, while the programme board brings together a wealth of practical lived experience and expertise from across the sector. I'm currently awaiting further advice from both groups on the role of wildlife and wildlife interventions, amongst other topics, and I look forward to considering the evidence base and their advice carefully. I also intend, by the way, to publish that advice to inform the wider debate.

I understand the frustrations of those who believe that progress has not been fast enough, and yes, I share those frustrations as much as anyone else. However, it is important that we get this right and that our decisions are grounded in robust evidence, alongside consideration of effectiveness, practicality, deliverability, animal welfare and value for money for the taxpayer. We must also recognise that some progress has been made in Wales. Let's not forget that more than 95 per cent of Welsh herds are officially TB free. That, I have to say, reflects the substantial efforts and hard work of farmers themselves, the vets that they work with and officials across Wales. I think we should always recognise that those efforts are ongoing.

But the challenge we face now is to build on that progress and push forward towards TB eradication in Wales. Innovative projects in Pembrokeshire and north Wales, for example, demonstrate the value of collaboration, stronger engagement between farmers and their vets, and local tailored action. I know that just as no two farms are the same, no two herd TB breakdowns are the same, and the measures to keep TB out of individual herds will also be different again. I commend the work of both of these projects and recognise the positive feedback that they're generating. The knowledge and experience from both of those projects will help inform future policy development. Picking up on some comments made about us knowing what we need to do and that the evidence is there, as Anna Nicholl told us, the science isn't static. That's why we have brought scientists, vets and world-renowned experts together in the form of the technical advisory group. They've travelled halfway around the world to come to Wales to help us deal with this situation, and it's constantly evolving. We're constantly learning from those local projects, from experiences in other parts of the UK and beyond. It's only right that we let the experts advise us and not think that politicians know best.

With regard to the proposed amendment, I welcome the constructive approach taken by the Member in recognising that progress has been made over recent years. However, you can't deny that the programme board's position paper, which was published in March, was clear that a step change is needed if we are to meet our TB eradication target here in Wales. Without that, more animals, more farmers, more farming families will experience the distress caused by TB breakdowns for longer.

contributions.item_title_en: 8. Welsh Conservatives Debate: Deposit-return scheme
contributions.text_english:
Now, deposit-return schemes are an internationally proven way to increase recycling, to collect high-quality materials, to support reuse, and that is important, and, of course, to reduce the environmental impact of single-use drinks containers. And for Wales, this offers us an opportunity to build on our recycling success by helping to commence the transition to reuse, drawing from the proven success, as I said, of some of the world's best schemes that are out there. So, getting this scheme right is about ensuring the scheme will work for Wales so that it delivers clear return on investment and brings real benefits to producers, retailers and consumers.

Now, while there may be different views on aspects of the scheme design, I think we can all agree on the shared ambition to introduce a successful deposit-return scheme that works for Wales, whilst being interoperable with the other schemes in the UK. The position on the scope of the scheme has been established, of course, with the Senedd having passed the regulations that are now in law, including the inclusion of glass and the phasing in of reuse. Reopening these fundamental elements would only create further uncertainty and certainly delay the October 2027 launch date being called for by industry, and the benefits that DRS can bring to Wales as well would subsequently be delayed.

Now, I would like to directly address some factually inaccurate claims that I've seen circulating about the costs of this scheme. Let me be clear: figures cited of a DRS in Wales costing £200 million or adding 50p to the price of drinks in glass bottles are not accurate. They relate to industry's upper estimate of the potential cost of fraud in the absence of a scheme in Wales. They don't reflect the scenario that we are working to, and we are clear on the need to bring in a scheme in Wales in parallel with those elsewhere across the UK. In line with the well-being of future generations Act requirements, it's important that we're also taking a long-term view, with DRS playing an important role as an investment in a more sustainable circular economy for Wales longer term.

Businesses have been clear that they need certainty and for the scheme to be delivered in parallel, as I say, with the schemes in the rest of the UK, and the regulations provide a clear framework for industry to prepare, to invest and plan with confidence, and we are committed to working in partnership with industry to deliver the scheme by October 2027. And as has been quoted—as a Government, our manifesto commitment is clear—whilst glass is in scope from the outset, the full requirements in relation to glass need to be implemented pragmatically and when feasible, particularly for SMEs.

So, we're therefore committed, as I say, to working with industry to ensure the practical implementation of the regulations, and we're fully committed to interoperability with schemes across the UK. And with international examples having already demonstrated that variations in scope within a shared single market are entirely deliverable, so interoperability shouldn't be confused with uniformity, and the need to ensure that Wales has a scheme that works for us, as well as the rest of the UK, is perfectly achievable. There are examples; somebody mentioned Finland earlier, and there was reference to a long border in Wales. The Finnish border is about 20 or 30 times longer than the situation we have in Wales. We have US states, of course, that have interoperability that work to very different systems.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch yn fawr, Ddirprwy Lywydd. I mentioned the US states as well. You know, they are in a similar position. Those aren't the same hard borders that you believe exist everywhere. These schemes can be and will be interoperable. Large tracts of the regulations in Wales actually mirror word for word the regulations in England. It's a journey that we're on. I know exactly where we want to get to, and there's a trajectory that we need to see happening. Wales was given the ability to include glass. We do have the United Kingdom Internal Market Act 2020 because it was seen as an opportunity to see how that could be developed and how that could work, and I'm keen to achieve that, but as I say, working with the industry and working with the people of Wales who have already showed an ambition to go further.

I want to make a point about the appointment of the deposit management organisation; that's where I was. Look, our aim is to take a balanced and pragmatic approach. I was saying that, combining long-term ambition with deliverability, and we currently are working at pace to complete the formal process of appointing a deposit management organisation. There was an assertion made earlier that we had rejected—we hadn't. That had happened under the former Government. We are now picking up from there, and I'm optimistic that we will bring this to a positive conclusion in short order. My focus, and that of my officials, is firmly on making sure that the organisation appointed will be able to deliver a scheme that works in Wales, and it would be inappropriate for me to prejudge the outcome or to comment on any individual applications, because, obviously, the appointment has to be made through a fair, transparent and robust process in line with the regulations. But, as I say, I hope to bring a positive conclusion to that in short order.

As we have learned from international schemes, the appointment of an effective management organisation is a critical milestone in implementation, as once they're appointed, they play a pivotal role, of course, in working with producers, retailers and wider stakeholders to oversee delivery, to provide certainty to the industry and to help ensure that the scheme is launched successfully, as is planned in October 2027. And as has already been mentioned, the scheme in Wales is necessarily different because, of course, our starting point on recycling is very different. We are focused on putting in place a scheme that delivers clear benefits to Wales.

One of my colleagues, Carrie Harper, said in a discussion last week on fair funding that today's underinvestment becomes tomorrow's disadvantage, and the same applies here to the economic opportunities associated with a DRS scheme and the wider circular economy. If Wales is required to wait for others to catch up, then we risk missing out on potential investment, on potential jobs, and the benefits that we're already seeing in our wider economy from our status as one of the best recycling nations in the world. Too often, decisions affecting Wales are made elsewhere by organisations whose priorities might conflict with Welsh interests. Wales should be able, of course, to shape our own future, but we also should be able to capture the value of our own resources and realise the economic benefits of the transition to a circular economy here in Wales, rather than seeing those opportunities accrue elsewhere.

These decisions aren't always the easiest, I accept that, but they are the right ones, and I believe the people of Wales expect us to show that leadership. Ultimately, our goal, necessitated as I say by our current cycling rates, isn't simply to deliver a DRS for recycling, which everybody has been talking about, but it's one that supports Wales to move up the waste hierarchy, so that drink containers are used and reused again and again, so that valuable resources remain in circulation, so that producers can then benefit from a reduction in the materials needed to package their drinks, and so that the people of Wales can also benefit from the environmental improvements and economic opportunities that this is already bringing to other countries and regions around the world.

contributions.item_title_en: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
contributions.text_english:
Well, there's no agenda from this Government when it comes to driving down livestock numbers. I can give you that assurance. Agriculture is central to the strength of our rural economy, and it's absolutely critical to the resilience of our rural communities. This Government is clear that Wales needs a strong, sustainable and productive livestock sector. We want to see Welsh farmers producing high-quality food in a way that's both economically and, yes, environmentally sustainable. The sustainable farming scheme is a part of achieving that, including through the sustainable production optional action, which will help farmers improve productivity and long-term resilience whilst continuing to produce Welsh meat to the high standards that we all expect.

When we look at agriculture's climate impact, we have to look at the whole picture. The agriculture inventory records emissions doesn't fully reflect the wider contribution the sector makes—through carbon sequestration, for example. There's a huge contribution that is being made, and more that can be made, in that space, and we need to be looking at maximising those opportunities, to take pressure off other elements within the sector.

So, there's no agenda to drive down livestock numbers from myself or this Government because the kind of food system that we want to see, the kind of food economy that we want to see in Wales, will be based on local production, local processing and local procurement. We therefore need to maintain and strengthen each element of that. So, processing and livestock numbers, the throughput numbers, is part of that, so that we can deliver a strong, sustainable and productive livestock sector, because that is a big, big priority for me.

contributions.item_title_en: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
contributions.text_english:
Thank you for the question. It gives me an opportunity, I think, to reiterate an important point here, which is, I think, the thrust of your question: whilst we are keen to reduce bureaucracy and red tape, that in no way takes us away from the importance of many of the regulations and protections that we have, because they're there for a purpose, and we need to make sure that they are respected and carried through and delivered upon.

What I'm not happy with is the bureaucratic burden that comes with some of those processes. So, I've said from the start, if we can take duplication out of the system—and there is duplication, we're already seeing that a few weeks into this red tape review, that there is duplication. If the Government is asking for data and information, then, are we confident that we're using it? Because, if not, frankly, why are we asking for it? These are the questions that we need to ask. Not, fundamentally, 'Do we want to row back on some of the standards, the high standards, that we insist on across the piece in Wales?' And those high standards are important, because they're a big part of what Welsh food and Welsh produce is about: it's high quality, high environmental standards, high animal welfare standards. We need to retain those.

Where I'm persuaded that we need regulatory change, it'll be on the basis of making life easier and more practical, but I won't be sacrificing some of those fundamental principles that we have around the environment and animal health and welfare, et cetera—that's not the driver here; that's what I'm trying to say. The driver here is to make life easier for farmers whilst fulfilling the regulations and the aspirations that we have for the outcomes that we want to see.

contributions.text_english:
The Welsh Government will protect our rivers, but we will do that by taking control of water in Wales so that we can strengthen regulatory oversight, improve accountability of water companies and drive better environmental performance across our rivers, lakes and seas. As I said, there's no disagreement about the scale of the challenge that we face; water quality in Wales is not where we want it to be. While progress has been made, only around, as we heard, 40 per cent of water bodies in Wales currently meet good ecological status. That underlines how far we have come, but certainly how much further we need to go.

Public concern is high and people rightly expect urgent and visible action. I agree with the public strength of feeling. We want clean water, we want a healthy environment and we want a system that delivers for communities, not one that tolerates failure. That is why the Welsh Government is taking forward a comprehensive programme of water reform, which is focused on three things: taking control of our water, strengthening regulatory oversight and company accountability, and improving environmental performance.

At the heart of our approach is a simple principle, and that is that decisions affecting Wales should be made in Wales. The First Minister has already made that case to the Prime Minister, because this is about ensuring that Wales has the capability to act decisively in the interests of our people and our environment. A central part of this reform is ensuring that regulation reflects the reality of devolution and isn't stuck in the past. The current system, of course, is based on an outdated 'wholly or mainly' model, which no longer aligns with the way Wales is governed.

We're working with the UK Government to align water regulation with Wales's geographic border, and good progress has been made. I hope to confirm more about that shortly. This is about clear accountability, it's about coherent regulation, and, of course, for all of us here, it's about stronger democratic oversight for customers as well, on both sides of the border. This Government will reset how Wales manages water. We will create a clearer, more coherent system for Wales that supports long-term strategic decision making, that directs investment to Welsh priorities, and strengthens regulatory oversight in Wales. This isn't just about structural change; we want to see better outcomes for Wales.

Under a Welsh-focused regulatory framework, companies will be subject to clearer expectations, stronger performance oversight and more direct consequences when they fail to meet standards. This includes the ability to set price controls for Wales, it includes delivering value for money for Welsh customers, and direct investment to priorities determined here in Wales. We will honour our manifesto commitment that water company bosses should not receive bonuses where companies fail to meet the standards the public rightly expect.

Let me be clear: where companies fall short, they must face consequences, and customers must not bear the cost of putting things right. But in improving water quality, we have to be honest about the nature of the problem. Sewage discharges are a major concern, but they are not the only issue. We know, as many have acknowledged in the debate, that agriculture and rural land use is part of the problem, so it needs to be part of the answer. But the point I'm making is that there is no single cause of it, so there is no single solution here, and that's where our approach will need to be a whole-system approach.

We're working with water companies to reduce sewage spills and improve infrastructure, but we're also working in partnership with Natural Resources Wales, farmers in Wales and the agricultural sector to deliver those sustainable solutions that reduce pollution at source whilst also supporting a resilient rural economy. This includes moving towards a more science-led, outcomes-based and risk-proportionate approach, moving away from the blunt farming-by-calendar approach, which is clearly not working. We will replace rigid one-size-fits-all rules with a system that better targets high-risk activity—yes, that needs to be targeted—but also better supports good practice.

We're also strengthening catchment-based approaches through nutrient management boards and wider partnerships to bring together regulators, farmers, water companies and local authorities to deliver co-ordinated action on the ground, including, of course, through nature-based solutions. Because the reality is this: lasting improvements in water quality will only be achieved if everybody plays their part.

Dirprwy Lywydd, this is a longer term programme of reform, and it's essential that we deliver it in a way that maintains stability for customers, but also confidence for investors. The Welsh Government is working closely with the UK Government on the forthcoming clean water Bill, which is expected later this year, which will devolve powers to the Senedd to enable us to establish a new regulator. But we're also working with the UK Government to bring forward the necessary legislative consent motions in a timely way, making sure that decisions affecting Wales are subject to Senedd scrutiny here in this Chamber.

Now, alongside this, we're co-developing a transition plan with the UK Government to make sure that there are no gaps in regulation or any disruption to services as we move towards the new system in Wales, and that transition plan will provide stability through this period of change while sending clear signals to regulators and companies about all our expectations. So, once we have the powers, we can bring forward legislation within this Senedd term and that is exactly what I intend to do. And I look forward to all Members here playing their part in scrutinising that legislation, and making it the strongest legislation it can possibly be.

Subject to these processes, we expect a new regulatory system to be established in the early 2030s, aligned with future price review cycles, and designed to deliver long-term environmental and economic outcomes for Wales. But while reform progresses, we won't wait to act. We will continue to strengthen monitoring of pollution incidents, and I will seek assurances from Dŵr Cymru, from Hafren Dyfrdwy, from Natural Resources Wales, Ofwat and others that robust action is taken where failures occur.

Dirprwy Lywydd, this Government's position is clear: we will take full control of water in Wales, we will strengthen accountability and we will deliver a water system that protects our environment, that supports our communities and meets the expectations of the people of Wales now and for generations to come. I therefore ask Members to please support our amendment to this motion. Diolch.

Thank you very much, Deputy Llywydd. I'm very pleased to make this statement today to explain my priorities for my portfolio. In a week, of course, where we are experiencing a red weather warning for heat for the first time here in Wales, I'd like to start with our commitment to take action on climate and nature, not only because of its environmental importance, which is clear to all, but also because of its central importance to the future prosperity, health and resilience of Wales in the future. Clean air, clean water, healthy soils and thriving ecosystems are not optional extras. They support public health, they protect communities and create the conditions for Wales to develop sustainably.

This agenda is about delivering on the positive economic opportunities from Wales’s natural resources and our global status as a recycling nation. It's about taking the opportunities of a zero-carbon economy to support secure jobs, community energy, warmer homes, cleaner transport, sustainable food production, and resilient infrastructure. This is why, during our first 100 days, we have already started work on an ambitious climate and nature action plan, focused on a practical pathway to net zero by 2040 and substantive nature recovery by 2050, shaped by the realities people and communities are facing across Wales.

Those realities are clear. Farmers, for example, need land that is productive and resilient, not land that is repeatedly under floodwater or under pressure because of drought time and time again. Children and families also should be able to enjoy clean beaches and seas. Businesses need access to resilient supply chains. Future generations should inherit a Wales where nature is recovering, not one where species are disappearing in our lifetimes. The plan will embed action on climate and nature as Cabinet-level responsibilities across all portfolios, so that it is built into decisions on housing, transport, energy, health, the economy, and public services.

contributions.text_english:
The plan is about delivery. We'll improve resilience to climate impacts while supporting opportunities for skilled well-paid jobs, community energy, warmer homes, better infrastructure and a fair transition for all. The plan will bring together the practical steps needed to reduce emissions, restore nature and strengthen resilience. This will include also action on tree planting and peatland restoration, recognising their vital role in restoring habitats, improving water quality, reducing flood risk, as well, of course, as tackling climate change. We will therefore deliver the national peatland action programme and prioritise native woodland creation, restoration and mixed woodlands, while protecting productive agricultural land and avoiding corporate plantations created solely for carbon offsetting. We'll support small-scale planting, whilst recognising the importance of commercial timber production. Using public procurement and working in partnership with industry, we will help develop Welsh supply chains and work together to deliver the timber industrial strategy. Our natural environment doesn't stop at the shoreline. Our seas support rich marine life, sustainable fisheries and aquaculture, tourism, coastal communities and the responsible expansion of offshore wind and marine renewable energy. A healthy marine environment is central to climate resilience and nature recovery.

By embedding action on climate and nature across Government, we will ensure that the need to decarbonise, improve resilience and restore nature is reflected consistently in policy, funding and in delivery. The Environment (Principles, Governance and Biodiversity Targets) (Wales) Act 2026 gives us important tools to do this. Our focus is now on embedding environmental principles into policy making, setting clear outcomes for nature recovery and establishing the Office of Environmental Governance Wales to provide independent oversight. By moving to a circular economy that keeps resources in use and avoids waste, that will not only reduce emissions and protect nature by reducing pressure on global resources, it will also capitalise on the economic opportunities that flow from our world-class recycling. This, in turn, will strengthen our supply chains, and it'll also reduce exposure to volatile global markets, whilst attracting investment to support skilled jobs.

We're also committed to driving forward water reform, including plans for a new Welsh economic water regulator with the powers needed to drive investment, to reduce pollution and to deliver long-term improvements. Taking a science-led approach to managing nitrate vulnerability, we will move beyond the outdated calendar-based rules and support farmers to adopt new technologies and practices that improve water quality. To deliver on our agenda, we will work collaboratively across sectors in partnership with local government and public bodies and drawing on the skills and experience of people working across Wales, including in not-for-profit organisations.

Now, as part of our commitment to restoring biodiversity whilst creating jobs and strengthening the connections between communities and their natural environment, I’m pleased to announce that the Nature Networks fund will open on 9 July. That will see £10 million of investment delivered in partnership with the National Lottery Heritage Fund. However, public funding alone can't achieve our climate and nature objectives. We will, therefore, consult later this year on our approach to nature finance, to unlock responsible private funding to restore land and seascapes, to support the Welsh economy and to create employment opportunities.

Within our first 100 days, we will also outline the terms of reference for a new flood resilience and preparedness forum for Wales, bringing together key stakeholders to coordinate a national approach to flooding. Flooding is already, as we know, affecting homes, businesses and communities as part of a wider pattern of climate pressures, from more intense rainfall and storms to drought, heat and pressures on water, land and infrastructure. We need a joined-up approach to preparedness and improved long-term resilience. This includes catchment-scale and nature-based solutions that reduce risk, that protect communities, support nature recovery and help Wales adapt to the climate impacts that we're already experiencing.

We'll also continue to press the UK Government on environmental justice for coalfield communities, including the funding needed to restore coal tips and contaminated land. Communities living with the legacy of Wales’s industrial past should not be left to carry that risk alone. We will take a long-term, co-ordinated approach to secure these sites, safeguard communities and, of course, unlock their future potential. 

I now want to turn to rural resilience. Dirprwy Lywydd, for me, this is about listening to rural— and coastal, by the way—communities, and recognising people, place and opportunity: the homes people live in, the services they rely on, the businesses they build, the food they produce, and the landscapes and seascapes that shape their lives. Within our first 100 days, we will, therefore, bring forward proposals for a new statutory duty on rural-proofing, ensuring Government programmes, funding models and services properly reflect the needs of rural communities. And this will sit alongside the development of a rural development strategy to start tackling poverty and to create new opportunities in rural Wales.

I firmly believe that the agriculture sector is the beating heart of our rural communities and the backbone of the rural economy. Family farms sustain local businesses and services; they underpin our food system, as well as our culture and our language. Through the sustainable farming scheme, we're asking farmers to join us on a journey to a more resilient and sustainable agricultural sector. Now, this year, as Members know, 50 per cent of farmers—that's over 8,000 businesses—have joined the universal layer of the scheme. Now, that's quite a positive start, in my view, but I will continue to listen and to work with the farming community to refine the scheme, so that more join next year and beyond. As I've said before, this is about evolution, not revolution. Farmers, of course, need certainty, and that's particularly the case when it comes to financial support, and that's why I'm currently in discussions about securing a multi-annual budget for the sustainable farming scheme.

Bovine TB, as we all know, remains one of the most significant and persistent challenges facing agriculture in Wales. We will refresh the TB eradication programme, building on strong foundations, but recognising that a step change is needed to meet our ambition of a TB-free Wales by 2041. Building on Wales’s already strong record on animal welfare, we will also bring forward a new animal health and welfare plan, including new regulations for animal welfare establishments.

contributions.text_english:
I also, Dirprwy Lywydd, want to decrease the bureaucratic burden on family farms, making a real difference to the time that is spent on complicated and duplicated processes—time that could otherwise be spent managing stock, improving productivity or, of course, planning for the future. I have asked John Davies to lead an independent review to identify areas of unnecessary complexity and actions to reduce that.

Supporting farmers alone, of course, is not enough. We will also be championing Welsh fisheries, supporting the industry as a vital part of Wales’s food system and coastal economy. We must also strengthen the system that brings food to people across Wales. We will be doing this through a new national food strategy for Wales, safeguarding food supply chains, improving food literacy, strengthening supply chains and supporting our food and drink industry to grow, building on our reputation for high-quality, sustainably produced food.

We have a clear vision: a Wales where action on climate and nature strengthens our economy, improves the health of our people and protects our communities, where strengthening rural and coastal areas and making them more resilient is at the heart of everything this Government does, where our farmers and our fishers are valued for the hard work that they do to put food on our tables, where our food system works for the benefit of the people of Wales. We all need to work together to realise and implement this vision. I, of course, will be open about the challenges we will of course face along the way, but I will also focus on the opportunities to build a more resilient, healthier and more prosperous Wales, working with communities, farmers, businesses and public services to deliver practical change that is shaped, of course, by the people who know their communities best. This is the journey that is ahead of us: listening, shared responsibility, practical delivery and long-term resilience for Wales. I very much hope that Members in this Chamber will join us on that journey. Thank you.
